particulars: All names, dates, places, ages, counts (stab wounds, victim height, number of confessions, sentence lengths, 21-day limit) and the identities of the governors and the real perpetrator were dropped.

items.record: The accused's intellectual disability made him compliant: "to compensate for his disability, Washington would politely defer to any authority figure"
items.reading: Lists mental capacity as unknown and says nothing confirms it.
items.loss: The suspect's personal vulnerability, which explains how the confession was produced, is missing.

items.record: Police said he had confessed to several crimes at once, and most were thrown out: "the first four were dismissed by the Commonwealth because of the inconsistencies"
items.loss: The interrogation produced confessions to many crimes, and the institution itself discarded most of them while keeping one.

items.record: The confession got key facts wrong: "did not know the race of his victim, the address... or that he had raped her"
items.reading: Says the statement was steered until it matched the theory, so it sounded orderly and sincere.
items.loss: The confession stayed visibly wrong rather than polished, and the authorities accepted it anyway.

items.record: The confession was rehearsed until accepted: "Only on the fourth attempt at a rehearsed confession did authorities accept"
items.reading: Speaks generally of leading questions and corrections.
items.loss: The concrete process was repeated rehearsal until a version was signed off and signed.

items.record: Police led him to the scene: "taken there three times in one afternoon by the police, who in the end had to help him pick out Williams' apartment"
items.loss: Investigators directly built the corroborating evidence through a staged site identification.

items.record: Forensic evidence was altered after he became a suspect: "an amended forensic report was prepared (without additional testing being conducted) that said... 'inconclusive'"
items.reading: Suppression is described only as unpursued leads and dismissed recantations.
items.loss: Exculpatory lab results were actively rewritten, not just ignored.

items.record: The trial was one-sided: "only the State's psychologist testified" and "the defense did not offer any counter argument... concerning a sentence of death"
items.loss: The defense failed at trial and the expert evidence was uncontested, which is a source of the wrongful outcome the reading never names.

items.record: The case carried a death sentence and an execution date: "secured a stay of execution for Washington nine days before he was scheduled to die"
items.reading: Mentions appeals and imprisonment, never capital punishment.
items.loss: The stakes were life or death, and the case came within days of an execution.

items.record: Rescue came through a fellow prisoner and a volunteer: "another death row inmate, Joseph Giarrantano, alerted Marie Deans (a non-lawyer...)" and a lawyer who happened to be there brought the case to her firm
items.reading: Guesses at a lone defense attorney, an innocence project, a relative, a journalist or online sleuths.
items.loss: The specific chain of chance contacts inside prison that started the challenge is missing.

items.record: Exoneration was blocked by procedure, not by official doubling-down: "time barred by Virginia law... he was not exonerated. Instead... commuted"
items.reading: Says the institution escalated exponentially, hardening with each new doubt.
items.loss: The real obstacle was a rigid deadline on new evidence, and DNA proof still did not free him.

items.record: Relief came through executive clemency, in stages: commutation, then a "pardon... on limited grounds," release to parole, then an "absolute pardon" years later
items.reading: Predicts vacatur, exoneration or quiet dismissal through the courts.
items.loss: Governors, not courts, resolved the case through a slow series of partial steps over many years.

items.record: Release was conditional: "released from prison to parole supervision"
items.loss: Even after the pardon, he remained under state supervision rather than being fully free.

items.record: The real perpetrator confessed: "Kenneth Tinsley... pleaded guilty to Rebecca Lynn Williams' rape and murder"
items.reading: Mentions an alternate suspect only as one possible source of doubt.
items.loss: Full acknowledgment of innocence came only after the actual offender admitted the crime.

items.record: The dying victim's only description was racial: "could only describe her attacker as a Black man acting alone"
items.reading: Treats the accused's race as unknown and the victim's role as unknown.
items.loss: A race-only description from the victim framed the search for a suspect.

items.record: He was brought in on unrelated charges: "arrested in nearby Fauquier County, for an alleged burglary and malicious wounding"
items.loss: He became a murder suspect through an unrelated arrest, not through any evidence tying him to the killing.

items.record: His reaction to release was mild: "This was a whole lot better than I expected."
items.reading: Describes his experience as disorienting, then hopeless.
items.loss: The accused's own understated, accommodating voice is missing.
